published_title: THE WORD THAT HAD NO SECOND SPEAKER

story.title: THE WORD THAT HAD NO SECOND SPEAKER
story.deck: A three-hundred-year-old treaty turns on one word that a mining company reads as lease and a valley reads as lend, and only one living person speaks the language. Illuminara has nine days, a court that wants a translator, and a witness who will not be made into a key.
story.shape: Five scenes across nine days: a refusal that closes the easy road, three uses of the word gathered from keepers who have never compared notes, a sealed prediction table with the company’s fallback built in, a blind handing back of three objects under three readings, and a ruling that moves the mine and puts the word into children’s mouths.

scenes.title: Eighty-nine
paragraphs: *Kessel Reach tribunal, hearing room two · Day One, 08:10*

The Compact of the Seven Springs ran to four pages, and the whole of it turned on a single word of the Irú language. Harrow & Vane Minerals read the word as lease. The people of the Irú valley read it as lend. Between the two readings lay a ridge, the aquifer under the ridge, and seven thousand people who drank from it.

The word was oruma. The tribunal had nine days to say what it meant, and no dictionary could help it. The last Irú school had burned with its books, and the last person who spoke the language with the weather and the work still in it sat in the front row under a grey blanket. Ilo Marrow was eighty-nine. He had been asked to testify six times and had refused six times.
Pell Ardent, the court’s translator, stood by the bench with a folder of field recordings and the look of a woman who had not slept. She spoke to Illuminara without turning her head.

**Pell Ardent**  
Counsel for the company telephoned me at home last night. She said a reading of lease would be very much in keeping with the recordings. I said I would read what the recordings said. She said she was sure I would.

**Illuminara**  
Did you hear a threat?

**Pell Ardent**  
I heard someone checking how much weight I could carry. If I am the only voice, I will be the weight.

Illuminara had once been paid to carry words across a courtroom without letting them change on the way. She knew what the bench wanted from her, and it was a second voice. One speaker could be doubted. Two would be a record. There was no second.
She went down the aisle and knelt by Ilo’s chair so that he would not have to look up.

**Illuminara**  
I can interpret for you. I have done it in courts. I would not change a word.

**Ilo Marrow**  
You are kind, and you would make me a quotation. I would speak, you would speak, and the court would keep yours.

**Illuminara**  
Then I will not ask what the word means.
His eyebrows rose a finger’s width.

**Illuminara**  
I will ask what a person does after hearing it.
Ilo looked at his hands for a long time, spotted and knuckled, the hands of a man who had lent a great many things.

**Ilo Marrow**  
That is a question for a seed. I will speak to objects, girl. I will not speak to you about them.
Wren Odira, who had kept the court’s clock since the first morning because nobody else would, wrote 08:41 in her notebook and beside it, *objects only*.

scenes.title: What a Person Does Next
paragraphs: *Three hamlets of the Irú valley · Days Two to Four*

The language was nearly gone, but the practice had not died with it. Illuminara walked to three people who lived a day’s walk apart, had never compared notes, and spoke only the common tongue: Teodora Brisk at Upper Haddow, whose cress and barley trays went from house to house each spring; Hamid Sorel, warden of the reservoir boats; and Anke Doyle, who lent the names of dead grandmothers to newborns and took them back. Wren drove the borrowed truck and wrote down where each of them stood.
She asked each the same question in the same words. What does a person do after you say oruma?

**Teodora Brisk**  
You take the measure in March. In May you bring it back with a handful over. And you say what failed.

**Hamid Sorel**  
The boat goes out leaking. It comes home caulked, with your name cut in the new plank. Nobody hands back a boat the way they found it. That is how I know they used it.

**Anke Doyle**  
The name comes back with a line on the board. What the child did with it.
Three trades, three ways of returning, one shape: use, change, account. Illuminara set the shape aside as a hypothesis, not an answer, and asked each of them the question that could break it.

**Illuminara**  
What if the borrower hands it back exactly as found?
Teodora, Hamid and Anke made the same small face, three days and thirty miles apart.

**Teodora Brisk**  
Then they are telling me they never touched it. Or that they hid what they did.

Illuminara wrote that down and then went looking for her best enemy. Ines Calder, counsel for the company, had put one document into evidence that she believed nobody could answer: oruma of the reservoir ferry right to the Crowe family in 1794, never called back in two hundred and twelve years, and no object ever returned.

**Hamid Sorel**  
The log came back. Every winter the Crowes carried the ferry log up to the council hall. That is what coming back looks like when the thing is a river.

**Wren Odira**  
It fits the company’s second reading if you squint. Keep the thing, send a token. You told me to say when something fits.

**Illuminara**  
It fits mine if you do not squint. That does not make it proof. It makes it the place where the test must be able to fail.

scenes.title: Three Columns
paragraphs: *Tribunal annex · Day Five, 07:30*

Illuminara spread one sheet across the annex table and drew two columns before anyone could object to the first. LEASE: a fixed term, a fee, the thing returned as found. LEND: use, then the thing returned changed, with an account, and the lender free to call it back. Under each she wrote what a borrower would do with a measure of seed, a skiff and a name-board when the season ended.

**Ines Calder**  
Performing a gloss in a courtroom shows what the performers believe. I will oppose it.

**Illuminara**  
So the performer will be your surveyor, who has never heard the word spoken by anyone who meant it. And the judges will be three keepers behind a screen who will not know which protocol they are watching. Correct the lease column if I have drawn it unfairly.

Calder read the lease column slowly. She struck one line, corrected another, and then, unprompted, drew a third column and headed it GRANT: the thing kept, a token sent home each year. It was her fallback, and she wrote it down where the tribunal could see that she had one.

Maren Tolliver, the company’s surveyor, who had walked Ridge Nine for eleven years and was said to know the aquifer better than the hydrologists did, agreed to do the handing back. She asked one thing.

**Maren Tolliver**  
Who decides whether I did it right?

**Illuminara**  
Not Ilo. If this rests on one old man, it is a quotation again. Each keeper decides for the thing they keep. If a keeper cannot decide, that handing back counts as unresolved, and it does not count for me.

**Wren Odira**  
And if he will not say anything to an object?

**Illuminara**  
Then the record says he refused. A refusal is not an answer, and I will not turn it into one.

The nine handings back, three protocols on three objects, would be drawn from a hat. The envelope held three predictions that mattered. The keepers would call LEND closed. They would call LEASE not closed. And GRANT they would push back across the table, because a thing kept is a sale. Wren signed across the flap at 07:52.

scenes.title: The Surveyor’s Hands
paragraphs: *Upper Haddow seed house · Day Six, 10:00*

A linen screen divided the seed house, with a slot cut low in it that showed only hands and the thing in them. On one side sat Teodora, Hamid and Anke at separate tables, each with a pencil and a card marked CLOSED and NOT CLOSED. On the other stood Maren Tolliver with her sleeves rolled, and Ilo Marrow in a chair beside a measure of barley seed, a skiff with a weeping seam and a pine name-board scored with nine names.
Each time, Ilo spoke a short phrase to the object in Irú, not to the woman, and each time Illuminara wrote down only the time. She did not translate. Tolliver did what the sheet in her hand said.

Under the lease protocol she paid the fee and handed the seed back exactly as found, measure for measure. Teodora looked at it for a long moment and turned her card to NOT CLOSED. Under the lend protocol Tolliver had run a germination test on the ridge soil with the seed, and she returned the measure with a handful over and a page of what had rotted. Teodora turned her card to CLOSED and pushed the measure to the middle of her table, where a lender sets down what she has received.
The skiff went the same way. As found, the seam still wept, and Hamid ran a thumb along it.

**Hamid Sorel**  
Leaking. Exactly as it was. She never got in it.

He marked NOT CLOSED. Under lend she had caulked the seam in an hour and cut her name in the plank, and he marked CLOSED. Under grant she kept the skiff and sent home one nail, and Hamid pushed the nail back through the slot with a forefinger. Ask the price, the gesture said, and the rule that had been written the day before scored it NOT CLOSED.

At the name-board, under the lend protocol, Tolliver cut a line of account into the pine. Ilo spoke to the board for longer than the formula needed, quietly, in a voice that was not for the room. Illuminara wrote *untranslated, Ilo to the board* and nothing else.

**Wren Odira**  
What did he say?

**Illuminara**  
A man spoke to a board. I will not make it into something he said to me.

By one o’clock the envelope was open. All nine of the keepers’ calls on their own objects matched the prediction. Of the twenty-seven calls the three keepers made together, twenty-five matched. The two that did not were Teodora and Hamid, who had both marked the name-board GRANT as CLOSED, reasoning that a single token line was a faint account. Anke, who owned the board, had marked it NOT CLOSED and drawn a small question mark beside it. Illuminara entered the handing back as unresolved and did not smooth it.
Calder had watched the lease handing back all morning with her arms folded.

**Maren Tolliver**  
I did not think of doing it any other way than as found. In my trade that is clean. In theirs it is a lie.

**Ines Calder**  
You were asked to perform a word you do not speak.

**Maren Tolliver**  
I was asked what a decent person does with a borrowed thing. Three people who have never met told me. I did not need Irú for that.

scenes.title: The Dry Shoulder
paragraphs: *Kessel Reach tribunal, hearing room two · Day Nine, 15:20*

Judge Anselm Rhee read for forty minutes. He said the tribunal did not hold that a demonstration was a dictionary, and that Ilo Marrow’s sentence to the board would stay in the record as untranslated. He found, on the evidence of practice from three independent keepers, a prediction sealed before the test, a hostile reading allowed to fail, and one surveyor’s honest hands, that oruma obliged an account and a return changed by use, and carried the lender’s right of recall. No account could be given of a mine above the aquifer that returned the springs unharmed. Harrow & Vane’s claim to Ridge Nine reverted to the valley.

He then read the council’s offer, made in open session on Day Seven: the Dry Shoulder, a bare saddle of rock south of the ridge, with ore a third thinner, lent to the company on the same word and on the same terms of account.

**Ines Calder**  
I have advised my client not to appeal. Our own surveyor’s hands are in the record. We ask only that the account be annual, and that recall be written out, so that no one on either side has to guess what the word means in a bad year.

It was an expensive sentence for her to say. At the Dry Shoulder four hundred mining jobs would never exist. Oren Basque, the council speaker, who had wanted the whole ridge and the company gone from it, signed with a hand that shook. The Vesper and Hale families lost the summer pasture on the saddle and left the hall without speaking to anyone.
The tribunal’s last order directed the company to fund a school. Ilo Marrow answered it from his chair, in the common tongue, before the judge had finished.

**Ilo Marrow**  
I will not be paid for it. I will lend it. Nine people, and each of them takes one thing, a seed or a boat or a name, and brings it back changed.
Pell Ardent read the order into the record without a folder. Maren Tolliver asked, from the back of the hall, whether she might be counted among the nine, and nobody laughed.

At 16:04, on the courthouse steps, Ilo put a measure of seed into the hands of the youngest of them, a girl of seven called Pia, and said the word to her, not to the seed. Pia answered in Irú, loudly and wrongly, and the old man laughed until he coughed.

**Wren Odira**  
That is a second speaker.

**Illuminara**  
That is a first one. He needs nine more, and then they need each other.
Wren wrote the time. The word had had one speaker for a long season, and by spring it would have ten.

scenes.title: Three Columns
paragraphs: *Tribunal annex · Day Four, 07:30*

Illuminara spread one sheet across the annex table and drew two columns before anyone could object to the first. She left the third column blank and turned the sheet to face Ines Calder.

**Illuminara**  
Write your best reading. Not the one that is easy to beat. The one a careful lawyer would defend in her sleep.
Calder took the pen. She did not write the lease Illuminara had expected, a fee and the thing returned as found.

**Ines Calder**  
A lease allows wear. The tenant maintains, at her own cost, and keeps a written account of the days she used it. The thing comes back sound, and the lessor does not take it back before the term runs, for any reason, because that is what a term is.
She headed the column LEASE and underlined *any reason*.

**Illuminara**  
Your column and mine agree on the seed, the skiff and the name-board. A tenant mends the seam and cuts a line on the board too.

**Ines Calder**  
Then your objects cannot tell us anything.

**Illuminara**  
They can tell us whether the keepers recognize their own rules. They cannot tell us where we part, and we part in one place. Can the lender call it home before the term, if she has to?
Calder was silent for a breath. Then she did what Illuminara had not asked, and chose the case.

**Ines Calder**  
A sluice paddle from the reservoir office, lent for the term of the hearing. Mid-term, the lender calls it back. Twice: once because the water is rising, once for no reason at all. Beneath them she wrote the line she wanted Calder to see: *If Mr Crowe closes the tenant’s hold against a flood, I withdraw the claim of recall and the tribunal may enforce the account alone. If he closes it only against a whim, I narrow the claim to the flood.* The Day Nine ruling depended on it. If recall fell, so would the ridge.
At 09:15 Tolliver took the objects. Wren logged the minute she sowed two trays of cress, ridge soil and valley soil. Forty-eight hours, said Teodora, was a cress season.

scenes.title: The Surveyor’s Hands
paragraphs: *Upper Haddow seed house · Day Six, 10:00*

The gate needs its paddle.* Under the lender’s protocol Tolliver returned the paddle with her log of days used, and Brann Crowe, who had said nothing since he sat down, marked it CLOSED. Under the tenant’s she said the term ran to Day Ten and offered the fee for the lost days. Crowe looked at the paddle for a long moment and marked it NOT CLOSED.

At 12:10 the second notice came through. *The lender wants it back.* Nothing more. Tolliver returned the paddle at once, and her hands, which had been quick all morning, were slow with it. Crowe marked it NOT CLOSED. Under the tenant’s protocol she held the paddle to the term, and he marked it CLOSED.
Wren opened the envelope at one o’clock. Illuminara had called two of the four recall marks wrong.

So it is a lease. A lease holds against a whim.

**Brann Crowe**  
It holds against a whim. It does not hold against a flood. My people never called the ferry because it never stopped coming home with the log. If anyone had called it for no reason, I would have told them where to put the log.

**Ines Calder**

I was asked what a decent person does with a borrowed thing. Four people who have never met told me, and one of them was your witness. I did not need Irú for that.

He had been asked to testify six times and had refused six times.
Pell Ardent, the court’s translator, stood by the bench with a folder of field recordings and the look of a woman who had not slept.

**Pell Ardent**  
Counsel for the company telephoned me at home last night. She said a reading of lease would be very much in keeping with the recordings. I said I would read what they said. She said she was sure I would.

**Illuminara**  
Did you hear a threat?

**Pell Ardent**  
I heard someone checking how much weight I could carry. If I am the only voice, I will be the weight.
She knew what the bench wanted from her, and it was a second voice. One speaker could be doubted. Two would be a record. There was no second.
She went down the aisle and knelt by Ilo’s chair so that he would not have to look up.

**Illuminara**  
I can interpret for you. I have done it in courts. I would not change a word.

**Ilo Marrow**  
You are kind, and you would make me a quotation. I would speak, you would speak, and the court would keep yours.

**Illuminara**  
Then I will not ask what the word means.
His eyebrows rose a finger’s width.

**Illuminara**  
I will ask what a person does after hearing it.
Ilo looked at his hands for a long time, the hands of a man who had lent a great many things.

**Ilo Marrow**  
That is a question for a seed. I will speak to objects, girl. I will not speak to you about them.
Wren Odira, who kept the court’s clock because nobody else would, wrote 08:41 in her notebook and beside it, *objects only*. Under it she ruled a line and wrote *216 h from 08:00*.

scenes.title: What a Person Does Next
paragraphs: *Three hamlets of the Irú valley · Days Two and Three*

The language was nearly gone, but the practice had not died with it. Illuminara went to three people who lived a day’s walk apart, had never compared notes, and spoke only the common tongue: Teodora Brisk at Upper Haddow, whose cress and barley trays went from house to house each spring; Hamid Sorel, warden of the reservoir boats; and Anke Doyle, who lent the names of dead grandmothers to newborns and took them back.
She asked each the same question in the same words. What does a person do after you say oruma?

**Teodora Brisk**  
You take the measure in March. In May you bring it back with a handful over. And you say what failed.

**Hamid Sorel**  
The boat goes out leaking. It comes home caulked, with your name cut in the new plank. Nobody hands back a boat the way they found it. That is how I know they used it.

**Anke Doyle**  
The name comes back with a line on the board. What the child did with it.

Use, change, account. Illuminara set the shape aside as a hypothesis. These three had described the practice her columns were drawn from, so they could not also be the people who proved the columns right.

At Hamid’s desk she stopped him turning a page. His boat-book, Exhibit Fourteen, had been logged as a repair ledger and nobody had read it for a verb. The oldest entry was 1727, a year after the Compact.
*Skiff, oruma to Aldous Sorel for the fishing, the plank to be cut and the boat to come home. Called home in the flood of 1731. It came.*

She laid Clause Four beside it. The same frame stood in both: the word, a holder, a use, and a clause saying what must happen at the end. The ferry grant Ines Calder had put in evidence herself, *oruma to the Crowes for the crossing, the log to be borne up each winter*, carried it too. It had never been called back in two hundred and twelve years.

**Wren Odira**  
It fits the company’s second reading if you squint. Keep the thing, send a token. You told me to say when something fits.

**Illuminara**  
It fits mine if you do not squint. That does not make it proof. The frame shows the word came with an ending-clause. It does not show that the clause was a debt, or that anyone could call it early. For that we need a case nobody on my side has built.

**Hamid Sorel**  
The Crowes carry the ferry log up to the council hall every winter. That is what coming back looks like when the thing is a river.

scenes.title: Three Columns
paragraphs: *Tribunal annex · Day Four, 07:30*

Illuminara spread one sheet across the annex table and drew two columns. LEND: use, then the thing returned changed, with an account, and the lender free to call it back. GRANT: the thing kept, a token sent home each year. She left the third column blank and turned the sheet to face Ines Calder.

**Illuminara**  
Write your best reading. Not the one that is easy to beat. The one a careful lawyer would defend in her sleep.
Calder took the pen. She did not write the lease Illuminara had expected.

**Ines Calder**  
A lease allows wear. The tenant maintains, at her own cost, and keeps a written account of the days she used it. The thing comes back sound, and the lessor does not take it back before the term runs, for any reason, because that is what a term is. The springs are rendered whole when the term ends, and the account says how.
She headed the column LEASE and underlined *any reason*.

**Illuminara**  
Your column and mine agree on the seed, the skiff and the name-board. A tenant mends the seam and cuts a line on the board too.

**Ines Calder**  
Then your objects cannot tell us anything.

**Illuminara**  
They can tell us whether the keepers recognize their own rules. They cannot tell us where we part, and we part in one place. Can the lender call it home before the term, if she has to?
Calder was silent for a breath. Then she did what Illuminara had not asked, and chose the case.

**Ines Calder**  
A sluice paddle from the reservoir office, lent for the term of the hearing. Mid-term, the lender calls it back. Twice: once because the water is rising, once for no reason at all. And the judge is not one of your three keepers, who have heard your table. Brann Crowe. His family has held the ferry for two hundred years, and he has no reason to love you.
Maren Tolliver, the company’s surveyor, who had walked Ridge Nine for eleven years, agreed to do the handing back. She asked one thing.

**Maren Tolliver**  
Who decides whether I did it right?

**Illuminara**  
Not Ilo. If this rests on one old man, it is a quotation again. Each keeper decides for the thing they keep, and Mr Crowe the paddle. If a judge cannot decide, it counts as unresolved, and it does not count for me.

At 07:52 she wrote her predictions on a card and Wren signed across the flap. The lender’s protocol would close both recalls; the tenant’s would close neither. Beneath them she wrote the line she wanted Calder to see: *If Mr Crowe closes the tenant’s hold against a flood, I withdraw the claim of recall, and the company may blast Ridge Nine and answer for the springs in a ledger at the end of the term. If he closes it only against a whim, I narrow the claim to the flood.* Everything on the ridge hung on that card. A spring that was fractured in the third year could not be rendered whole in the tenth.
At 09:15 Tolliver took the objects. Wren logged the minute she sowed two trays of cress, ridge soil and valley soil. Forty-eight hours, said Teodora, was a cress season.

scenes.title: The Surveyor’s Hands
paragraphs: *Upper Haddow seed house · Day Six, 10:00*

A linen screen divided the seed house, with a slot cut low in it that showed only hands and the thing in them. On one side sat Teodora, Hamid and Anke at separate tables, each with a pencil and a card marked CLOSED and NOT CLOSED, and at a fourth table Brann Crowe, lean and unsmiling. On the other stood Maren Tolliver with her sleeves rolled, and Ilo Marrow beside a measure of seed, a skiff and a pine name-board scored with nine names. Forty-eight hours and forty-five minutes had passed since the sowing.

Each time, Ilo spoke a short phrase to the object in Irú, not to the woman, and Illuminara wrote down only the time. Tolliver did what the sheet in her hand said, and she did not know which protocol came next.

Under the tenant’s protocol the seed came back sound, measure for measure, and Teodora marked it CLOSED. Under the lender’s it came back with a handful over and a germination page, the ridge-soil tray grey with rot beside the green valley tray, and Teodora marked that CLOSED too. Under grant Tolliver kept the measure and sent home one seed, and Teodora did not turn her card at all. The skiff went the same way, and for the grant one nail that Hamid pushed back through the slot with a forefinger. At the name-board Tolliver cut a line of account into the pine, and Ilo spoke to the board for longer than the formula needed, quietly, in a voice that was not for the room. Illuminara wrote *untranslated, Ilo to the board* and nothing else.

**Wren Odira**  
What did he say?

**Illuminara**  
A man spoke to a board. I will not make it into something he said to me.
Anke wrote a question mark beside the grant. That was the one call the keepers could not make, and Illuminara entered it as unresolved.

At 11:30 the usher carried a notice through the slot, in Hamid’s hand. *The water is rising. The gate needs its paddle.* Under the lender’s protocol Tolliver returned the paddle with her log of days used, and Brann Crowe, who had said nothing since he sat down, marked it CLOSED. Under the tenant’s she said the term ran to Day Ten and offered the fee for the lost days. Crowe looked at the paddle a long moment and marked it NOT CLOSED.

At 12:10 the second notice came through. *The lender wants it back.* Nothing more. Tolliver returned the paddle at once, her hands slow with it. Crowe marked it NOT CLOSED. Under the tenant’s protocol she held the paddle to the term, and he marked it CLOSED.
Wren opened the envelope at one o’clock. Two of Illuminara’s four recall marks were wrong.

**Ines Calder**  
So it is a lease. A lease holds against a whim.

**Brann Crowe**  
It holds against a whim. It does not hold against a flood. My people never called the ferry because it never stopped coming home with the log. If anyone had called it for no reason, I would have told them where to put the log.

Illuminara struck *free to call it back* from her own column and wrote above it, *for need*. She entered the miss as a miss. She had predicted that the lender could call the thing home. The case had said: for need, not for pleasure.

**Maren Tolliver**  
My hands found a difference, and not the one I expected. Holding the paddle to the term, I was doing business. Putting it down when the water rose, I was paying a debt I had not known I had. Held through a term, or returned for a need somebody shows you. That is all my hands could tell apart.

**Ines Calder**  
You were asked to perform a word you do not speak.

**Maren Tolliver**  
I was asked what a decent person does with a borrowed thing. Four people who have never met told me, and one of them was your witness. I did not need Irú for that.

scenes.title: The Dry Shoulder
paragraphs: *Kessel Reach tribunal, hearing room two · Day Nine, 15:20*

On Day Seven the council had offered the company the Dry Shoulder, a bare saddle of rock south of the ridge, with ore a third thinner, lent on the same word and the same terms of account. Tolliver’s own 2019 cores from the saddle were already Exhibit Nine, and Calder had confirmed the grade by eight that night. Had she not, Wren’s notebook said, the tribunal would have ruled on the ridge alone at noon on Day Eight.

Judge Anselm Rhee read for forty minutes. He said a demonstration was not a dictionary, and that Ilo Marrow’s sentence to the board would stay in the record untranslated. He took the matter in three parts and said which was which. On the word, the 1727 boat-book, the 1794 ferry grant and Clause Four shared one frame: continuity was proved. On the obligation, the keepers’ practice and Mr Crowe’s marks showed a debt of account and a return changed by use. On recall, the single 1731 entry and Mr Crowe’s marks carried it for need and not for whim, a judgment under uncertainty, which the tribunal held.

Then he said what the holding was for. A lease without recall let Harrow & Vane blast through its term and answer for the springs in a ledger at the end, when Clause Four’s promise to render them whole would fall due on a fractured aquifer no ledger could mend. A loan recallable for need let the valley call the springs home while they could still be returned, and the lower spring had fallen to a third of its winter flow. The springs had called. Had Mr Crowe closed the tenant’s hold against the flood, the tribunal would have ordered the account alone, and the company would have blasted. Harrow & Vane’s claim to Ridge Nine reverted to the valley.

**Ines Calder**  
I have advised my client not to appeal. Our own surveyor’s hands are in the record, and I wrote our own column. We ask only that the account be annual and that recall for need be written out, so that no one on either side has to guess what the word means in a bad year.

At the Dry Shoulder four hundred mining jobs would never exist. Oren Basque, the council speaker, who had wanted the company gone from the whole ridge, signed with a hand that shook. The Vesper and Hale families lost the summer pasture on the saddle and left without a word.
The tribunal’s last order directed the company to fund a school. Ilo Marrow answered it from his chair, in the common tongue, before the judge had finished.

**Ilo Marrow**  
I will not be paid for it. I will lend it. Nine people, and each of them takes one thing, a seed or a boat or a name, and brings it back changed.
Pell Ardent read the order into the record without a folder. Maren Tolliver asked, from the back of the hall, whether she might be counted among the nine, and nobody laughed.

At 16:04, on the courthouse steps, Ilo put a measure of seed into the hands of the youngest of them, a girl of seven called Pia, and said the word to her, not to the seed. Pia answered in Irú, loudly and wrongly, and the old man laughed until he coughed.

**Wren Odira**  
That is a second speaker.

**Illuminara**  
That is a first one. He needs nine more, and then they need each other.
Wren wrote the time. The word had had one speaker for a long season, and by spring it would have ten.
